newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU crude stock rise seen equalling fall in products.
newsitem.headline: EU crude stock rise seen equalling fall in products.

text.p: European oil inventory figures for the end of April, to be released on Tuesday, are likely to show a balanced picture as rising crude stocks cancel out falling gasoline and distillate levels, analyst said.
"It looks like (stock levels) will be flat overall," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at bank UBS in London.

The largest draw is likely to have been in middle distillate stocks. Analysts estimated that the fall in April could have been as much as 10 million barrels after Asian buying took out a large volume of Russian material.
The figures for the 15 countries of the European Union plus Norway will be published by Euroilstock at 1300 GMT on Tuesday.
"Gas oil's going to be very interesting given the movement of product out of the area, but it should be down," said Cindy Poynter of oil consultants Bonner and Moore.

Nevertheless, she, like others, believes the draw will only be a token comfort against the depressing look of gas oil stocks viewed year on year. Asian demand has since faded and European buying, in the meantime, has been poor.
"Without that pull from Asia, we would have seen a real weakening...The market is still fundamentally poor with about four days of supply more than the historical average," Poynter said.

Gasoline stocks likewise are expected to have fallen as the United States absorbed product, notably at the start of the month. Analysts estimated the draw will be between four and eight million barrels in April.
"This time of year is normally the period of maximum draw. Product certainly did go to the States, so we would expect to see at least the normal draw of gasoline," Pyne said.
Crude stocks by contrast are expected to have risen as supplies increased and continued refinery maintenance limited throughput.
Some analysts noted that Iraq increased crude exports sharply in April to reach the six-month limit allowed by the United Nations under the $2 billion oil-for-food deal.

"There was a lot of supply, especially at the start of the month. Don't forget that the increased contango in the market also encouraged stock building," said Colin Birch, principal consultant at Purvin and Gertz.
